summary:
North Sulawesi stands under the national framework applicable across Indonesia. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with reporting indicating that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, and in Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; North Sulawesi is not among the provinces with that regime.

Provincial divergence for a visitor in North Sulawesi is not documented. OutRight Action International's 2022 study of national laws and regional regulations examined eight focus provinces, Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta, finding significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear; North Sulawesi is not among the eight, and the Sulawesi entry in that set is South Sulawesi, a different province. The study states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set, but it records no North Sulawesi regulation.

No sourced record of an enforcement incident, raid, arrest, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people in North Sulawesi was located. The visitor-facing risk profile therefore follows the national picture: the new KUHP in force since January 2026, with police extortion and arbitrary detention the main documented mechanism of pressure. Venue raids remain a national enforcement form, as on 22 June 2025 when Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena stated that the gathering violated no law.

Police conduct toward LGBT people in Manado has been documented locally. A 2016 account from SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the provincial LGBT organisation, records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people, including a butch lesbian who was groped during a raid, and that victims often do not report because they fear their families will not accept their orientation. That account records no arrests or prosecutions.

Two further national factors bear on what a trans visitor may face. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022 and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, which Indonesian police deny, and she was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists LGBTQ+ people among nonmilitary threats within national defence policy, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women.
tangentialFactors:
Public LGBT presence in Manado is documented and long-standing. On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined the city's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, running from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA, with SALUT participating and its director Coco Jericho quoted. Visibility of this kind has coexisted with the raid conduct described in the same reporting.

Official-level engagement with the waria community in North Sulawesi has also occurred. On 10 November 2012 a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach in Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi (BNN) as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS; Sinjal was quoted saying waria are among local people and deserve attention. No adverse official action is recorded in connection with the event.

Compared with provinces that carry their own criminalising regime, North Sulawesi's exposure is the national one. Aceh's caning sentence of February 2025 and the provincial criminalisation in South Sumatra apply under local religious or provincial law and do not extend here, while the national morality provisions and the 2026 code do. National hostility is expressed through official framing as well as policing: commentators quoted by ABC News state that the October 2025 regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.
localsOnly:
North Sulawesi has an organised trans community with province-level representation. Alexa was elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara for 2016 to 2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado. In a Konde.co interview published in February 2024 she said that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. No legal or police action appears anywhere in her account.

Local LGBT organising continues through SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), which has spoken publicly about raid conduct and participated in city-wide campaigns. Reporting notes that residents who experience harassment during raids frequently do not report it, citing fear that their families will not accept their orientation, which limits the official record of incidents in the province.

OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping covers eight focus provinces and does not name North Sulawesi, and the study's statement that its findings are valid beyond the focus set is a general methodological claim rather than a specific finding about this province.

Unresolved: no sourced reporting after 2024 on police raids, arrests or prosecutions of LGBT or transgender people in Manado or elsewhere in North Sulawesi was located. The most recent local enforcement account dates to 2016, so current enforcement practice in the province is not established by these sources.

Not sourced: whether the national KUHP provisions in force since 2 January 2026 have been applied in North Sulawesi, and whether the October 2025 presidential decree on nonmilitary threats has produced any operational measures in this province. The vigilante attacks on transgender women reported in August 2026 are documented at national level without a stated provincial breakdown.
